constraints: Only unresolved contexts need to remain available.
A closing event always applies to the most recently opened unresolved context.

blocks.text: Each opening event pushes one unresolved context. A closing event must compare against the top because no earlier context may close while a newer nested context remains open. A queue exposes the oldest context and therefore reverses the required dependency. Recursion can internally use a call stack, but it is not required; the learning decision is the LIFO state rule itself.

messages.text: A queue is plausible because it also stores pending work, but it exposes the oldest pending context. It becomes valid only when the next action must serve arrival order rather than close nested work.
Recursion can create LIFO call frames, but the problem does not require recursive control flow. An explicit stack is sufficient whenever the input is processed iteratively.

feedback.reason: The decisive signal is “most recently opened and still unresolved,” which is exactly a LIFO boundary.

options.text: Keep unresolved contexts in a queue and inspect the front.
Keep unresolved contexts on a stack and inspect the top.
Use recursion; an explicit data structure cannot represent this rule.

prompt: A single-pass validator opens nested contexts and must close the most recently opened context that is still unresolved. Which state discipline matches that requirement?

constraints: A resolved record is never needed again.
Each record is pushed at most once.

blocks.text: The stack represents the unresolved suffix of the process, not a full historical log. Pushing introduces a record once; popping removes that particular stack entry once. Oldest-first service would require queue semantics, while retaining every processed record is unnecessary unless a separate audit requirement exists. This one-way lifecycle is also the basis for later amortized analysis.

messages.text: A full audit log may retain every record, but that is a separate requirement. The LIFO decision state needs only unresolved records.
Oldest-first service is a FIFO contract. It would justify a queue, not a stack.
After an entry is popped it is no longer in the stack. It can be removed again only if a new entry is pushed.
If resolved records never leave, the structure is being used as history rather than as the minimal unresolved state.
Without the newest-first dependency, LIFO is not the decisive state rule.

feedback.reason: A stack is sufficient because only the newest unresolved record is actionable, and resolved records leave the state permanently.

options.text: The next decision depends on the most recently added unresolved record.
The oldest unresolved record must always be processed first.
The same pushed record may be popped repeatedly without being pushed again.
A record may be removed permanently once it is resolved.
Every record must remain stored for the entire scan.

prompt: Select all statements that correctly describe why a stack is sufficient for a newest-first unresolved-state process.

blocks.text: After opening A and then B, the unresolved stack is [A, B] with B on top. Closing A first would cross the nesting boundary and leave B suspended inside a context that no longer exists. The stack may contain multiple active contexts, but one close event resolves exactly the top entry unless the contract explicitly states otherwise.

messages.text: Arrival order is a queue signal. It becomes valid only for oldest-first work, not nested closure.
The presence of multiple entries does not make one event resolve all of them. Bulk closure would need an explicit separate rule.

feedback.reason: Nested resolution closes B first because the most recent unresolved context is on top.

options.text: Close A, because A entered the process first.
Close both A and B because a stack stores all active contexts together.
Close B, because B is the most recently opened unresolved context.

prompt: A process opens context A, then opens context B, and then receives one generic close event. Which context must be closed first under a valid nested-state contract?

blocks.text: Both stacks and queues can hold pending requests, but their removal order is not interchangeable. A stack would repeatedly favor the newest request and could starve older work. Recursion says nothing about which pending request should be chosen. The transfer boundary is the service order, not the existence of a container.

messages.text: Recursive control flow does not establish oldest-first service. The required state discipline is a queue.
Removing one item does not make order irrelevant. A stack chooses the newest pending request, which violates the stated contract.

feedback.reason: The decisive requirement is oldest-first service, which is FIFO rather than LIFO.

options.text: A stack is still equivalent because both structures remove one pending request.
This is a FIFO boundary, so a queue matches the decision rule.
The requirement implies recursive processing rather than a queue.

prompt: A support system must always process the request that has waited the longest. Which conclusion is correct?

blocks.text: Each committed command can push either an inverse operation or the state needed to restore the previous version. Undo pops the newest entry and applies it. The command stream may be processed iteratively, and command values need not be ordered. A call stack is one possible runtime mechanism, but it is not the product-level decision being trained.

messages.text: Recursion is plausible because language runtimes use a call stack, but undo history is explicit application state and can be managed iteratively.
Monotonic order is useful for dominated-candidate problems, not for chronological undo. Undo order is determined by recency.

feedback.reason: Undo needs newest-first history, not recursive decomposition or numeric monotonic order.

options.text: The feature requires recursive functions because every stack operation is recursion.
The commands must be kept in monotonic value order before undo can work.
An explicit stack of inverse commands or prior states is sufficient.

prompt: An editor processes a flat stream of commands and must undo the most recent committed command. Which implementation conclusion follows from the requirement alone?

constraints: Each Back action pops exactly one history entry and makes it current.

blocks.text: The first pop removes B and makes it current; the second pop removes A. The same stack entry cannot be popped twice, and a queue would reverse the navigation order. This transfer works because Back is explicitly newest-first. A forward-history feature would require a separate stack or another state contract.

messages.text: That is FIFO history replay. It would skip the most recent prior page.
Once B is popped, that entry is gone. Repeating B would require pushing a new B entry.

feedback.reason: Each Back action consumes one newest history entry, so B is restored before A.

options.text: The controller restores B, then A.
The controller restores A, then B.
The controller restores B twice because B was most recent.

prompt: A navigation controller is on page C. Before visiting B it stored A, and before visiting C it stored B. The back-history stack is therefore [A, B] with B on top. What happens after two Back actions?

blocks.text: After C1, C2, C3, the first undo must remove C3, then C2, then C1. A stack stores only the unresolved history in the order needed by the next action. A queue, sorted order, or unordered set loses the required recency relation.

messages.text: FIFO would undo the oldest command first, reversing the required history order.
A set does not expose which eligible command was committed most recently.
Lexical or numeric sorting does not represent commit recency.

feedback.reason: Undo targets the newest still-active command, which is a direct LIFO requirement.

options.text: A stack of committed commands, with the newest command on top.
A queue that removes C1 first because it arrived first.
A sorted list ordered by command text rather than commit time.
A set, because any undone command is equally eligible.

prompt: An editor commits commands C1, C2, and C3. Undo must remove the most recently committed command that has not already been undone. Which state discipline matches?

blocks.text: After open(A), open(B), B is the top unresolved context, so close(B) is legal and removes B. A then becomes the top and can be closed. The stack stores the unmatched contexts; it does not need to retain already resolved openers.

messages.text: The nesting contract makes the most recent unresolved opener uniquely eligible.
Labels do not determine nesting ownership; opening order does.
Oldest-first would pair close(B) with A and violate proper nesting.

feedback.reason: Nested closure is newest-first: the latest unresolved opener owns the next legal close.

options.text: Each closer must match the most recently opened context that has not yet been closed.
Each closer must match the oldest open context so the structure is processed FIFO.
Each closer matches the numerically or lexically largest opener, regardless of nesting.
Open contexts have no order, so any pending opener may be removed.

prompt: A parser reads open(A), open(B), close(B), close(A). Which recognition fact makes a stack sufficient for validating the nested structure?

blocks.text: A stack would return the newest pending ticket and violate the service contract. Nothing in the requirement asks for nested resolution, nearest-value dominance, or a most-recent rollback. Recognizing the requested order is more decisive than the presence of a push-like insertion operation.

messages.text: No candidate domination or nearest-value query is present; ticket age is simply FIFO order.
Sequential processing does not imply nested unresolved contexts.
LIFO serves the newest ticket first, opposite to the stated oldest-first policy.

feedback.reason: Oldest-first service is FIFO, so it is a boundary case that should not be mislabeled as LIFO merely because a container is needed.

options.text: A FIFO queue is the matching state discipline.
A LIFO stack is required because every pending item has a last position.
A nesting stack is required because tickets can be processed one at a time.
A monotonic stack is required because ticket age is ordered.

prompt: A support system must process tickets in arrival order, oldest first, even when newer tickets are waiting. What is the correct classification?

blocks.text: Nested validation and undo both need the newest unresolved or reversible entry. Oldest waiting work is queue behavior. Permanently removing dominated candidates is a separate monotonic-stack proof and requires more than simple recency.

messages.text: This signal points to a monotonic stack, whose ordered candidate invariant is distinct from ordinary LIFO.
Oldest-first is FIFO and conflicts with newest-first resolution.
The newest pending context is exactly the entry exposed by a stack.
Rollback of the most recent pending state is a direct LIFO transfer.

feedback.reason: Ordinary LIFO follows recency, while FIFO follows age and monotonic stacks add an ordered-dominance invariant.

options.text: The next action always targets the most recently opened or unresolved context.
Undo removes the latest committed state that has not already been undone.
The next action must process the oldest pending item.
Candidates may be permanently removed because an ordered successor dominates them for a nearest-value query.

prompt: Select all problem signals that support an ordinary LIFO stack rather than a queue or monotonic stack.

blocks.text: The defining signal is last-in-first-out reversal of recent state. A queue matches arrival order, while sorting and prefix sums solve different relations.

messages.text: Arrival order is FIFO.
Range aggregation uses prefix state, not LIFO history.
Numeric order is not recency order.
